subject: economics
title: Elasticity Essentials
welcome_lead: Some shoppers shrug when prices rise; others bolt. Discover how elastic — or stubborn — demand really is.
meta_desc: GCSE Economics adventure on price elasticity of demand: definitions, formula and types.
final_note: Elasticity defined. Now sharpen your calculator!

concepts.def: Price Elasticity of Demand — sensitivity to price.
PED = 1 — % change in Q = % change in P.

walkthroughs.body_html: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Always take the absolute value (ignore the minus sign). If PED = 2, a 10% price rise causes 20% drop in quantity demanded — elastic.
Four key factors: substitutes (many = elastic), necessity vs luxury (necessity = inelastic), share of income (big purchase = elastic), time (longer time = more elastic, you can adjust).

Inelastic: insulin, petrol, salt, electricity. Elastic: holidays abroad, designer trainers, cinema tickets, Coca-Cola (with Pepsi nearby). GCSE tip: when asked to identify, always justify using one of the four determinants.

What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price — the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
PED measures how flexible or stretchy a product is.
PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Demand always falls when supply increases.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.

sequence.def: PED = 0; quantity does not change with price
